title: Agriculture, the Economy, and the Kansas City Fed
summary: Schmid's first communication after the July 29 hold, and a clear escalation: he closes by saying outright that he does NOT see the current stance as restrictive and that returning inflation to 2 percent 'will require tighter policy' — explicit hike advocacy, where every prior 2026 speech landed on a hawkish-but-patient hold. The argument is built to pre-empt the look-through case: he dismisses the June inflation deceleration as one data point flattered by oil, notes oil is rising again, and stresses that inflation ex-energy has run above the pace consistent with 2% for six straight months and at 3.2% y/y is HALF A POINT HIGHER than a year ago, 'broad-based and growing.' He then argues against the supply-shock excuse on principle — inflation is always supply AND demand, tariffs and cattle prices only passed through because demand was strong, and shocks are only transitory because the Fed reacts to them ('I am uncomfortable ever assuming that a burst of inflation will be temporary'). He applies the same logic to the AI buildout: relative-price arguments are no reason to discount an aggregate price index. On the other mandate leg he is relaxed — unemployment 4.2% in balance, weak payrolls explained by a barely-growing labour force, growth resilient with the Q2 dip a trade/inventory artefact. With labour in balance and demand strong, the entire policy burden falls on inflation and the conclusion is tightening.

key_quotes.quote: Given the strength of demand and investment, I do not see the current stance of monetary policy as restrictive. As such, I believe that bringing inflation down to the Fed’s 2 percent objective will require tighter policy.
key_quotes.context: The closing sentence and the marginal news: an explicit call for hikes, up from the hawkish hold of his Feb–Jul speeches

key_quotes.quote: Inflation excluding energy has run above the monthly pace needed to reach our inflation target in the six months before June. Over the previous 12 months, inflation ex-energy was 3.2 percent, about ½ percentage point higher than where it stood in June of last year.
key_quotes.context: The evidentiary core — underlying inflation is not just high but higher than a year ago, and 'broad-based and growing'

key_quotes.quote: I am uncomfortable ever assuming that a burst of inflation will be temporary. Inflation shocks are not intrinsically transitory. How persistent a spike in inflation is ultimately depends importantly on how the Fed reacts or is expected to react.
key_quotes.context: His reaction function stated explicitly: supply shocks are transitory ONLY because the Fed responds to them — the direct rebuttal to the look-through camp (Williams, Paulson)

key_quotes.quote: The labor market also appears to be roughly in balance. The most recent data for June had the unemployment rate at 4.2 percent, about in line with what most economists estimate is consistent with a labor market that is neither too tight nor too loose.
key_quotes.context: No employment-side constraint on tightening; slow payrolls attributed to a barely-growing labour force rather than weak demand for workers

key_quotes.quote: In my view, monetary policy works best when policymakers remain focused on aggregate price indexes and largely ignore the distribution of relative price changes occurring beneath the surface.
key_quotes.context: Refuses to discount AI-buildout price pressure as a relative-price phenomenon — the aggregate index is the target
